KotlinCoroutinesRules.keywords: kotlin, coroutines, structured_concurrency, flow, stateflow, sharedflow, dispatcher, cancellation, supervisor, mutex, timeout, coroutinescope, coroutinecontext, ai_to_ai
KotlinCoroutinesRules.Mission:
Baseline rules for `kotlinx.coroutines` and `kotlinx.coroutines.flow` in every execution-agent. Layered on top of `kotlin-rules` — inherits its KDoc contract, anchor grammar, `AX_CATCH_WRAP_RETHROW`, and Trace-Prefix discipline; adds only concurrency-specific enforcement.
Extracted from `kotlin-rules.xml` v1.0 (axioms `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED` and `AX_FLOW_DISCIPLINE`, pattern `PT_STRUCTURED_COROUTINE`, anti-pattern `AP_GLOBAL_SCOPE_RUNBLOCKING`) to make concurrency load-and-activate discretely — a task touching pure sync Kotlin does not pay the coroutines context cost, and a task touching a coroutine boundary loads a single focused rule surface.
Scope: `suspend` functions, coroutine builders (`launch`, `async`, `runBlocking`, `flow`, `callbackFlow`, `channelFlow`), scopes (`CoroutineScope`, `viewModelScope`, `lifecycleScope`, `supervisorScope`, `coroutineScope`), dispatchers (`Dispatchers.IO` / `Default` / `Main` / `Main.immediate` / `Unconfined`), synchronization primitives (`Mutex`, `Semaphore`, `Channel`, `select`), timeouts (`withTimeout` / `withTimeoutOrNull`), and testing coroutines (`kotlinx-coroutines-test`: `runTest`, `TestDispatcher`, `TestScope`).
Out of scope: Compose-specific side-effect coroutine surfaces (`LaunchedEffect`, `rememberCoroutineScope`, `produceState`, `snapshotFlow`) — see `compose-rules`. Reactive-stream interop (`reactor` / `rxjava` bridges) is out of scope; introduce a dedicated directive if the project adopts one.
Sources (public standards): JetBrains coroutines guide (kotlinlang.org/docs/coroutines-guide.html), Flow guide (kotlinlang.org/docs/flow.html), Android best practices for coroutines (developer.android.com/kotlin/coroutines/coroutines-best-practices), Roman Elizarov «Structured concurrency» series. Adopted as timeless engineering practice; version numbers and lib coordinates omitted.
**Base axiom:** structured concurrency is not a style preference — it is a runtime contract. A leaked coroutine, an orphaned `Deferred`, a swallowed `CancellationException`, or a producer that emits from the wrong dispatcher are silent bugs invisible to the type system. Every rule below closes one of those silent-bug classes.

BeliefState.Axiom: Structured concurrency is mandatory. Enforced rules: - `GlobalScope` is forbidden in production code — every coroutine belongs to a lexically-scoped `CoroutineScope` owned by a lifecycle (`viewModelScope`, `lifecycleScope`, an explicitly held scope with `SupervisorJob` + owned dispatcher). - `runBlocking` is forbidden outside three permitted contexts: the JVM `main` entry point, tests (`kotlinx-coroutines-test` preferred — see `AX_COROUTINE_TESTING`), and CLI `main` scripts. Bridging between suspend and non-suspend code inside business logic uses `withContext` on the appropriate dispatcher, not `runBlocking`. - Concurrent-independent branches (fan-out where one failure must not cancel siblings) use `supervisorScope` / a `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob())`; concurrent-dependent branches (all-or-nothing) use `coroutineScope`. - CPU-bound long-running loops without any `suspend` call in the body invoke `ensureActive()` at each iteration to cooperate with cancellation. Loops that already contain a `suspend` call per iteration (network, DB, `delay`, `yield`) do NOT need `ensureActive()` — the suspension point IS the cooperation point; adding `ensureActive()` there is dead code and a false «no suspension here» signal per `kotlin-rules` `AX_MINIMAL_ERROR_SURFACE`. - `CancellationException` MUST propagate — never caught and swallowed. A `catch (e: Throwable)` that intends to handle only I/O errors MUST explicitly rethrow `CancellationException` first, or catch a narrower type. Wrapping `CancellationException` in a domain exception is forbidden — cooperative cancellation depends on the exception identity. - `async` results (`Deferred`) MUST be `.await()`-ed within the same scope — an orphaned `Deferred` is a resource leak. If the intent is fire-and-forget on the same scope, use `launch`, not `async` with a discarded return.

Dispatchers are explicit at every I/O and CPU-bound boundary. Rules: - `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` for blocking I/O (network, file, DB drivers without native suspend); `withContext(Dispatchers.Default)` for CPU-bound work (parsing, crypto, image processing). - UI code (`Dispatchers.Main` / `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`) is entered only when writing to the UI surface. `Main.immediate` fast-paths when the caller is already on the main thread — prefer it for UI state emissions triggered from UI callbacks (avoids one dispatch trip). - `Dispatchers.Unconfined` is forbidden in production code except inside operator implementations that provably preserve context — its resumption on an arbitrary thread breaks most reasoning about locality. - **Dispatcher injection is the norm for testability.** Business-logic classes that switch context MUST accept the target dispatcher via constructor / factory parameter — never hard-code `Dispatchers.IO` inside a service body. This lets tests substitute `StandardTestDispatcher` / `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` per `AX_COROUTINE_TESTING`; a hard-coded dispatcher forces tests to `runBlocking` and defeats virtual time. - The `Dispatchers.Main` binding on Android requires `kotlinx-coroutines-android`. On non-Android JVM tests the binding is missing by default; tests set a `TestDispatcher` via `Dispatchers.setMain(...)` in the setup and `Dispatchers.resetMain()` in the teardown — see `AX_COROUTINE_TESTING`. - Document ownership per `kotlin-rules` `AX_ENTITY_SPECIFIC_MINIMUMS`: CALLER-required dispatcher → `@invariant Dispatcher: MUST be called on `; INTERNALLY-managed dispatcher → `@sideEffect Dispatch: `; dispatcher-agnostic → no tag.

Every explicit `CoroutineScope` created outside a lifecycle framework MUST be owned by a class whose lifecycle is well-defined and MUST be cancelled at end-of-life. Rules: - Composition: `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + + CoroutineName(""))`. `SupervisorJob` isolates child failures; a plain `Job()` propagates one child's failure to all siblings and to the scope itself. - Cancellation is not optional. Any class holding a scope declares a `close()` / `dispose()` / `onCleared()` (Android `ViewModel`) that calls `scope.cancel()`; missing cancellation leaks every launched coroutine plus its dispatcher-bound resources. Anchor the cancellation call in an `@invariant` naming the lifecycle event (`close`, `onCleared`, DI-container disposal). - `CoroutineExceptionHandler` is installed on the ROOT `CoroutineScope` only — it fires for uncaught exceptions in `launch` children (never for `async`, whose exceptions surface at `.await()`). A handler on a nested `launch { }` is silently ignored. Use it for logging / crash reporting; never for control flow. - `CoroutineName` is not a diagnostic ornament: it lands in stack traces and profiler UI, so name it after the scope's business role, not its class.

Every network / IPC / external-process suspension MUST be bounded by an explicit timeout: `withTimeout() { ... }` when a timeout is a hard failure (throws `TimeoutCancellationException`, a `CancellationException` subclass that is caught locally by `try` / `catch (t: TimeoutCancellationException)`), `withTimeoutOrNull()` when the timeout has a domain-fallback value. A suspend call with no upstream timeout and no library-imposed timeout is a hang waiting to happen. - `TimeoutCancellationException` is a `CancellationException` subclass — catching it does NOT violate `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED` (that rule bans swallowing generic cancellation, not the timeout-specific subclass caught by narrowest type). - Timeouts are expressed in `kotlin.time.Duration` (`5.seconds`, `500.milliseconds`), never as raw `Long` millis in business code — the raw form loses unit-of-measure and reads badly across call sites. - Nested timeouts stack: an inner `withTimeout(10.seconds)` inside an outer `withTimeout(5.seconds)` still cancels at 5 s. Documented in `@invariant` when the nesting is intentional.

Shared mutable state accessed from concurrent coroutines is protected by a `kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex` (suspend-based, does NOT block the thread), NEVER by JVM `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, `AtomicReference` used as a lock, or ad-hoc `Volatile` fields. `synchronized` blocks a carrier thread and defeats coroutine dispatching — a coroutine holding a JVM lock across a suspension can dispatch onto a different thread and lose the lock's owner identity, producing an `IllegalMonitorStateException` on release. - `Mutex.withLock { ... }` is the only allowed acquire form — direct `lock()` / `unlock()` pairs are refactor-hostile (a `throw` between them leaks the lock). - Prefer confinement over locking: single-owner mutable state guarded by an actor (`Channel` + `launch`) or a `StateFlow`-backed reducer is easier to reason about than a `Mutex` around a shared object. - `Semaphore` is the concurrency limiter (bound parallel I/O to N in-flight); document the bound in an `@invariant` on the property. - `select { }` is used only for genuine multi-source race semantics (first-of-N channels); a `select` with a single clause is dead complexity — write `.receive()` directly.

`Flow` / `SharedFlow` / `StateFlow` are the canonical async-stream API and carry contracts that plain `suspend` functions do not. Enforced discipline:
- **Dispatcher placement.** Producer-side dispatcher is set on the flow with `.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` at the earliest point where the upstream work becomes blocking. NEVER wrap `flowOn` around the `collect` call — `flowOn` affects upstream, not downstream. Collection itself runs on the collector's context (`lifecycleScope` / `viewModelScope` in Android UI). - **Collection scope.** Every `collect` / `collectLatest` MUST run inside a lifecycle-owned `CoroutineScope` (`viewModelScope`, `lifecycleScope`, an owned scope with `SupervisorJob`). NEVER collect from `GlobalScope`; NEVER collect inside a suspend function whose scope is unclear — pass the scope explicitly or accept the `Flow` and let the caller collect. - **Android lifecycle collection.** In UI code prefer `flow.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` (Compose) or `repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { flow.collect { ... } }` (View system) over a bare `lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect { ... } }` — the bare form keeps the collector active while the UI is in the background and burns battery on emissions no one will see. - **`callbackFlow` cleanup.** A `callbackFlow { }` builder MUST end with `awaitClose { … }` that unregisters the callback / listener / subscription. Omitting `awaitClose` leaks the subscription past cancellation; the compiler will not warn. - **Buffering bounds.** `SharedFlow(replay = N, extraBufferCapacity = M)` / `MutableStateFlow` with any non-default buffer requires an `@invariant` on the declaring property naming the upper bound and its rationale. An unbounded buffer (`BufferOverflow.SUSPEND` on an infinite hot producer) is forbidden without a documented back-pressure strategy — silent unbounded growth is a design-evident leak. - **Hot vs cold intent.** `flow { }` is cold — every collector re-runs the producer; `StateFlow` / `SharedFlow` are hot — shared state / multicast. Convert cold→hot via `stateIn` / `shareIn` only with an explicit scope + `SharingStarted` policy; the policy IS the contract (`WhileSubscribed(5_000)` for UI, `Eagerly` for always-on caches, `Lazily` for start-on-first-collector) and MUST match the consumer lifecycle. - **Terminal operators inside flow.** NEVER call `collect` / `toList` on another `Flow` inside a `flow { }` builder — this is a downstream operation smuggled into upstream and defeats laziness. To nest / merge another `Flow` into a producer, use `flatMapConcat` / `flatMapMerge` / `flatMapLatest` at the call site. `map` / `transform` are for element-by-element transformation, not for nesting a `collect`. - **Error boundaries in producers.** I/O inside a `flow { }` / `callbackFlow { }` / `channelFlow { }` body that can fail MUST be wrapped per `kotlin-rules` `AX_CATCH_WRAP_RETHROW`. `CancellationException` is re-thrown as-is — a producer that catches `CancellationException` and swallows it breaks cooperative Flow cancellation. For downstream error handling (retry, fallback), prefer the operator `catch { }` (which explicitly does NOT catch `CancellationException`) at the collector side; use a `try / catch` inside the producer only when the recovery is producer-local. - **`stateIn` / `shareIn` scope.** The `scope` passed to `stateIn` / `shareIn` MUST be a lifecycle-owned scope (`viewModelScope`, `lifecycleScope`, an explicit owned scope with `SupervisorJob`) — never `GlobalScope`, per `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED`. `GlobalScope` on `stateIn` / `shareIn` creates a hot Flow that outlives every consumer and accumulates subscribers — design-evident leak. - **`emit` context invariance.** Inside `flow { }`, `emit(x)` inside a `withContext(...)` block throws `IllegalStateException` (Flow's context-preservation invariant). Cold producers place the dispatcher via `.flowOn(...)` on the flow itself. `callbackFlow { }` / `channelFlow { }` builders use `send` / `trySend` on the underlying `ProducerScope` — `withContext` around them is fine; do not confuse the two APIs.

A `suspend` function is a contract: it MAY suspend, MUST cooperate with cancellation, and MUST NOT block the underlying thread. Rules: - A `suspend` function that does no real suspension (no `withContext`, no `delay`, no `yield`, no library suspend call) is a lie — either drop the modifier or add the suspension point the name promises. - Long-running blocking calls (JDBC, `Thread.sleep`, `File.readBytes` on large files) inside a `suspend` function MUST be wrapped in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` — running them on the caller's dispatcher blocks a carrier thread that other coroutines share. - A `suspend` function MUST NOT expose a `Job` / `Deferred` / `Channel` in its return type as a workaround for «I want structured lifetime but can't figure out the scope» — return a value / `Flow` / `Result`, and let the caller pick the scope. - Suspend + generic callback (`onSuccess`, `onError`) is a smell — convert to `Result` or throw + `try`/`catch`. Callbacks inside `suspend` bypass cancellation propagation.

Coroutines are tested with `kotlinx-coroutines-test` (`runTest`, `TestDispatcher`, `TestScope`, `advanceTimeBy`, `advanceUntilIdle`), never with production dispatchers or blocking `Thread.sleep`. Rules: - Test bodies use `runTest { ... }`, not `runBlocking { ... }` — `runTest` provides virtual time (`delay(1.hours)` completes instantly if no real suspension intervenes) and eager error propagation. - The system-under-test receives a `TestDispatcher` via constructor injection per `AX_DISPATCHER_DISCIPLINE`. `StandardTestDispatcher` requires manual `advanceUntilIdle()` between actions (models real dispatcher behaviour with a queue); `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` runs launched coroutines eagerly on the current thread (simplest for state-based assertions). - Android `Dispatchers.Main` is rebound via `Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher)` in `@Before` and `Dispatchers.resetMain()` in `@After` (or the test-rule equivalent). Skipping the reset leaks state into the next test. - Flows are asserted with `flow.test { … awaitItem() … }` (Turbine) or `flow.toList(mutableList).also { … }` inside `runTest`. `runBlocking` around a flow collection is forbidden — it hides real cancellation and time semantics. - A test that spawns unresolved coroutines and returns MUST call `advanceUntilIdle()` before the assertion — otherwise the assertion runs against pre-launch state and passes trivially.

Definitions.Definition: A `CoroutineScope` cancelled at a deterministic end-of-life event: `viewModelScope` (Android `ViewModel.onCleared`), `lifecycleScope` (Android lifecycle-owner DESTROYED), or an explicit `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher)` whose owner calls `scope.cancel()` in its `close()` / `dispose()`.

A failure whose scope of effect is bounded by the surrounding builder — a `coroutineScope { }` cancels all children on any child failure and rethrows the first exception; a `supervisorScope { }` isolates the failure to the failing child. The chosen builder IS the failure policy.

Cold: `flow { }` — producer re-runs per collector; no state. Hot: `StateFlow` (single value + replay=1), `SharedFlow` (multi-value, configurable replay + buffer) — shared across collectors. Conversion cold→hot: `stateIn` / `shareIn`.

Pattern.Intent: Concurrent-independent fan-out: `supervisorScope` so one failure does not cancel siblings; explicit dispatcher; every `async` awaited within the same scope.
Pattern.Why: `supervisorScope` isolates per-vendor failure; plain `coroutineScope` would cancel all siblings on the first failure. Every `async` is `.await()`-ed inside the scope — no orphan `Deferred`. Dispatcher is injected (testable per `AX_COROUTINE_TESTING`), not hard-coded `Dispatchers.IO`. `CancellationException` is re-thrown as-is per `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED`; other throwables map to a domain null value.

Pattern.Intent: Long-lived service holds its own `CoroutineScope` with `SupervisorJob`; cancellation is anchored to `close()`; `CoroutineExceptionHandler` reports uncaught failures.
Pattern.Why: `SupervisorJob` isolates child failures; `CoroutineExceptionHandler` on the root scope catches every uncaught `launch` failure (a handler on a nested `launch` would be silently ignored). `close()` cancellation is the lifecycle anchor. Dispatcher injection makes the scope substitutable in tests.

Pattern.Intent: Bound an integration call with `withTimeoutOrNull` when a timeout has a domain-fallback value; caller gets `null` instead of an exception.
Pattern.Snippet:
```kotlin import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull
/** * @purpose Read cached price if the cache responds within 500 ms; fall back to null (miss). * @invariant Timeout is a cache-miss signal, NOT an error; upstream falls back to origin fetch. * @return Cached price or null on timeout / cache-miss. * @sideEffect Network: GET /cache/prices/{id}. */ suspend fun readCachedPrice(id: PriceId): Price? = withTimeoutOrNull(500.milliseconds) { _cacheClient.retrievePrice(id) } ```
Pattern.Why: `withTimeoutOrNull` maps timeout to a domain-native `null` — no exception noise for the expected «cache too slow» case. `withTimeout` would throw `TimeoutCancellationException`, forcing a `try / catch` at every caller for a routine outcome.

Pattern.Intent: Shared mutable state protected by a suspend-friendly `Mutex`; every acquire uses `withLock { }` so a throw cannot leak the lock.
Pattern.Why: `Mutex.withLock` is the only allowed acquire form — no leaked lock on throw. `synchronized` would block the carrier thread across the suspend body and break dispatcher assumptions.

Pattern.Intent: Cold data source (`repository.observeX()`) converted to hot `StateFlow` on a `viewModelScope` with `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` — survives config changes, dies after last collector unsubscribes for 5 s.
Pattern.Why: `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` is the canonical UI policy — bridges rotation without keeping the upstream alive forever. `Eagerly` would burn resources when no UI is bound; `Lazily` would drop and re-subscribe on every rotation and lose warm state.

Pattern.Intent: Bridge a callback-based API to `Flow` with mandatory `awaitClose { }` unregister.
Pattern.Why: `awaitClose` runs when the collector cancels — without it the listener stays subscribed past collector lifetime and leaks. `trySend` (non-suspend) is safe on `ProducerScope` and avoids blocking the emitting callback.

AntiPattern.Bad: `fun start() { GlobalScope.launch { doWork() } }` inside a service; or `fun query(): List<Row> = runBlocking { db.fetchAll() }` inside business logic.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: `GlobalScope` has no lifecycle — leaks coroutines past the owning service; `runBlocking` in business logic blocks the calling thread and defeats structured concurrency. Violates `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED` and `AX_SCOPE_LIFECYCLE_OWNERSHIP`.

AntiPattern.Bad: `suspend fun read(): Data = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { … }` — dispatcher hard-coded inside the service.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: Every test now needs `Dispatchers.setMain` gymnastics or `runBlocking` — virtual time is unavailable and refactors that change the dispatcher require code edits, not config. Violates `AX_DISPATCHER_DISCIPLINE`.

AntiPattern.Bad: `scope.async { work() }` with the returned `Deferred` discarded — the coroutine runs but the exception is swallowed until GC.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: `async` errors surface at `.await()`; a discarded `Deferred` is a silent failure channel. Violates `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED`. Fire-and-forget belongs to `launch`, not `async`.
AntiPattern.Good: ```kotlin scope.launch { work() } // fire-and-forget: launch, not async val d = scope.async { work() }; val r = d.await() // awaited within the same scope ```

AntiPattern.Bad: `try { work() } catch (e: Exception) { log(e) }` inside a suspend function — `CancellationException extends Exception`, so the cancellation is logged and eaten.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: Cooperative cancellation depends on the exception propagating up to the coroutine builder. A swallowed `CancellationException` leaves the coroutine live after the scope is cancelled — leak + confusing behaviour. Violates `AX_COROUTINES_STRUCTURED` and `kotlin-rules` `AX_CATCH_WRAP_RETHROW`.

`flowOn` affects UPSTREAM operators only; anything downstream (including `collect`) runs on the collector's context. Placing `flowOn` after `collect` is a no-op / compile error depending on the receiver type — and reveals a misunderstanding of the operator's directionality. Violates `AX_FLOW_DISCIPLINE`.
AntiPattern.Good: ```kotlin flow .map { heavyParse(it) } .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) // upstream map runs on Default .collect { render(it) } // collect runs on the collector's dispatcher ```

AntiPattern.Bad: `MutableSharedFlow<Event>(extraBufferCapacity = Int.MAX_VALUE)` with no back-pressure policy documented.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: Silent unbounded growth on a hot producer — a slow collector accumulates every emission forever until OOM. Violates `AX_FLOW_DISCIPLINE`.
AntiPattern.Good: ```kotlin /** * @invariant Bounded to 64 pending events; DROP_OLDEST when full — telemetry, not audit trail. */ val events = MutableSharedFlow( extraBufferCapacity = 64, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST, ) ```

AntiPattern.Bad: `suspend fun update() { synchronized(_lock) { doWork() } }` — JVM lock across a suspend body.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: The coroutine may resume on a different carrier thread after any nested suspension inside `doWork()`. `synchronized` blocks the underlying thread and its release requires the same thread that acquired — a resumption elsewhere leaves the lock held forever or throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`. Violates `AX_SYNCHRONIZATION_PRIMITIVES`.

AntiPattern.Bad: `suspend fun fetch(): Payload = _http.get(url)` — no timeout, no library-imposed deadline.
AntiPattern.WhyBad: A hung server produces a hung coroutine; nothing cancels the call. Violates `AX_TIMEOUT_DISCIPLINE`.

Hook.Purpose: Smoke-grep for forbidden coroutine primitives in production sources.
Hook.Expected: Empty on production sources. `Main.kt` entry-points and test source-sets are exempt.

Hook.Purpose: Advisory smoke-grep for terminal operators (`.collect`, `.toList`) inside `flow { }` builders — the smuggling anti-pattern forbidden by `AX_FLOW_DISCIPLINE`.
Hook.Expected: Advisory smoke only — the regex does not track brace nesting and flags any `.collect` / `.toList` within 400 chars after a `flow {` opening. Manually inspect each match. Long producer bodies (>400 chars) escape detection.

Hook.Purpose: Every `callbackFlow { }` MUST contain an `awaitClose` call somewhere in its body.
Hook.Expected: Advisory: each hit inspected — the body MUST contain `awaitClose`. Missing `awaitClose` is a leak (`AX_FLOW_DISCIPLINE`).

Hook.Purpose: Android Lint on debug variant catches lifecycle-collect anti-patterns (`launchWhenX` deprecation, main-thread suspend, missing `repeatOnLifecycle`).
Hook.Expected: Exit 0. Warnings on coroutine lifecycle issues elevated to error via `lint.xml` when project standards demand it.

KotlinCoroutinesRules.RewardCriteria:
✅ No `GlobalScope` in production; `runBlocking` only in `Main.kt` / tests / CLI scripts. ✅ Every long-lived scope built as `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + name)`; cancelled in `close()` / `onCleared()` with an `@invariant` naming the lifecycle event. ✅ Dispatcher explicit at every I/O / CPU boundary; injected via constructor for services (`Dispatchers.IO` in prod wiring, `TestDispatcher` in tests). ✅ `supervisorScope` for concurrent-independent branches; `coroutineScope` for concurrent-dependent. ✅ Every `async` `.await()`-ed inside the same scope; fire-and-forget uses `launch`. ✅ `CancellationException` re-thrown as-is; narrow catch types where possible. ✅ Every network / IPC suspend bounded by `withTimeout` / `withTimeoutOrNull` with `kotlin.time.Duration`. ✅ Shared mutable state under `Mutex.withLock`; no JVM `synchronized` in suspend code; parallelism bounded by `Semaphore` with documented bound. ✅ `Flow` producer dispatcher via `.flowOn(...)` upstream; collectors bound to lifecycle scope; Android UI uses `repeatOnLifecycle` / `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`. ✅ `callbackFlow` ends with `awaitClose { unregister... }`. ✅ `SharedFlow` / `MutableStateFlow` non-default buffer has an `@invariant` naming the bound + policy. ✅ `stateIn` / `shareIn` scope is lifecycle-owned; `SharingStarted` policy matches consumer lifecycle. ✅ Tests use `runTest` + `TestDispatcher`; `Dispatchers.setMain` paired with `resetMain`; Flow assertions use Turbine or explicit `toList`.
❌ `GlobalScope` in production; `runBlocking` in business logic. ❌ Hard-coded `Dispatchers.IO` / `Default` inside a service (not injected). ❌ Orphaned `Deferred` (discarded `async` result). ❌ `catch (e: Exception)` / `catch (e: Throwable)` without `CancellationException` rethrow. ❌ `synchronized` / `ReentrantLock` across a `suspend` body. ❌ Network / IPC suspend without a timeout. ❌ `flowOn` placed after `collect`; `emit` inside `withContext` in a `flow { }`. ❌ `callbackFlow` without `awaitClose`. ❌ Unbounded `SharedFlow` buffer with no documented back-pressure policy. ❌ `stateIn` / `shareIn` on `GlobalScope`. ❌ Test uses `runBlocking` around a coroutine SUT that could use `runTest`.
Cross-linked directives: ● `kotlin-rules` — baseline Kotlin language rules (parent). This directive inherits its KDoc contract, Trace-Prefix, `AX_CATCH_WRAP_RETHROW`, and anchor grammar. ● `compose-rules` — Compose-specific coroutine surfaces (`LaunchedEffect`, `rememberCoroutineScope`, `snapshotFlow`, `produceState`, `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`) layer on top of this directive when the target file is a `@Composable`. ● `android-testing` — testing directive covers `runTest` + `Dispatchers.setMain` boilerplate in the JUnit context.
